title: 🜏 Apprentice Codex: Initiation
text:
Welcome, Apprentice.
You stand at the threshold of your initiation. Over the next twelve weeks, you will transition from a novice practitioner to a disciplined wielder of computational and theoretical arts. This codex defines your path, your rituals, and the expectations that govern your ascent.
Failure to follow the codex will result in chaos. Precision, rigor, and consistency are your allies.

title: 🜏 Apprentice Codex: Initiation
text:
🜂 I. The Three Trials (Internship Milestones)
Your progression will be marked by three formal rites of presentation.

🜁 Week 2 — The Awakening
Objective: Demonstrate understanding of the theoretical foundations of your quest.

20-minute presentation
Must clearly explain:

Core concepts underpinning the project
Key mathematical structures and assumptions





🜃 Week 7 — The First Convergence
Objective: Reveal your first experimental or computational results.

20-minute presentation
Must include:

Preliminary results
Methods used
A dedicated slide titled “Obstacles & Unknowns”, containing:

Concepts not yet mastered
Blocking issues (technical or theoretical)



This is not a weakness—it is a required signal of awareness.



🜄 Week 12 — The Final Transmutation
Objective: Deliver a complete and coherent narrative of your work.

20-minute presentation
Must include:

Problem statement
Methodology
Results
Interpretation and limitations


At this stage, you are expected to demonstrate autonomy and synthesis.

title: 🜏 Apprentice Codex: Initiation
text:
🜏 II. The Laboratory Infrastructure (Setup)
Your work must be structured and reproducible. Disorder is forbidden.

All artifacts must reside in a GitHub repository within the lab organization:

Source code
Presentation slides
Reports

The repository must contain:

A branch named: review
A report written in:

LaTeX or
Markdown


The repository structure should remain clean, modular, and documented.

title: 🜏 Apprentice Codex: Initiation
text:
🜍 III. Weekly Rituals (Workflow Expectations)
Your training is iterative. Each week follows a strict cycle.

🜁 1. The Council Meeting

One meeting per week with your supervisor(s)
You must come prepared with:

Progress
Questions
Blockers





🜃 2. The Code Offering

All code must be submitted via Pull Request (PR) to the review branch
Requirements:

Assign supervisor(s) as reviewers
Ensure code is functional and minimally documented
PR descriptions must be explicit and structured





🜄 3. The Living Manuscript

Your report is a living document
Each week:

Update it with new findings
Submit updates via PR to the review branch





🜂 4. The Dual Slides Rite
Each week, you must produce two slides, submitted with your PR and presented during the meeting:

Slide 1 — Knowledge Acquired

What you learned this week
Concepts understood
Progress made



Slide 2 — Shadows Remaining

What you do not understand
Questions
Ambiguities
Blocking points

Clarity about ignorance is a requirement, not a flaw.

title: 🜏 Python Good Practices — The Discipline of the Craft
text:
In this laboratory, Python is not merely a tool—it is an instrument of precision.
Code that is unclear, irreproducible, or poorly structured is considered unstable magic.
This page defines the expected standards.

title: 🜏 Python Good Practices — The Discipline of the Craft
text:
🜂 Environment Management — The First Rule
All projects must use isolated environments.

⚠️ Mandatory Tool: uv
You are required to use :contentReferenceoaicite:0 for:

Creating virtual environments

Managing dependencies

Installing packages



Why uv?

Extremely fast (Rust-based)
Unified toolchain (replaces pip, venv, pip-tools)
Deterministic dependency resolution
Simpler workflow



Minimal Workflow
# Create environment
uv init --python {python_version}

# Install dependencies
uv add numpy scipy torch

# Run a script
uv run python your_script.py

title: 🜏 Python Good Practices — The Discipline of the Craft
text:
🜁 Project Structure — Order Before Power
A project must be organized as follows:
project/
├── src/
│   └── your_package/
├── scripts/
├── tests/
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
└── .venv/

Key Principles

Use src/ layout to avoid import ambiguity
Separate library code from scripts
Always include a pyproject.toml

title: 🜏 Python Good Practices — The Discipline of the Craft
text:
🜃 Code Quality — Clarity Over Cleverness

Rules

Functions must be short and single-purpose
Variable names must be explicit
Avoid hidden side effects
Prefer readability over micro-optimizations



Formatting & Linting
Recommended tools:

ruff
black

Example:
ruff check .
ruff format .

title: 🜏 Python Good Practices — The Discipline of the Craft
text:
🜄 Reproducibility — No Uncontrolled Variance

All dependencies must be pinned
Experiments must be reproducible from a fresh clone
Random seeds must be controlled when relevant

title: 🜏 Python Good Practices — The Discipline of the Craft
text:
🜂 Testing — Trust, but Verify
Use:

pytest

Minimum expectations:

Core functions must have tests
Edge cases must be considered
Tests must run without manual intervention

uv run pytest

title: 🜏 Python Good Practices — The Discipline of the Craft
text:
🜏 Documentation — Knowledge Must Persist

Every module must have a docstring
Complex logic must be explained
Reports must reference the code that generated results

title: 🜏 Python Good Practices — The Discipline of the Craft
text:
🜏 Final Rule
If your code cannot be:

installed cleanly,
executed reproducibly,
and understood by another researcher,

then it is not complete.
Discipline in tooling and structure is not optional.
